notes.definition: In humans, sex is determined by one of the 23 pairs of chromosomes, the sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY).
explanation: Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes, 46 in total. Of these, 22 pairs carry genes that control characteristics only, such as eye colour or blood group. The remaining pair is different: it carries the genes that determine sex. These are called the sex chromosomes. In females the two sex chromosomes are the same and are both called X, so a female is XX. In males the two sex chromosomes are different: one X and one smaller Y, so a male is XY.

Gametes are made by meiosis, so each gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair, including one sex chromosome. Because a woman is XX, every egg cell she makes carries an X chromosome. Because a man is XY, half of his sperm cells carry an X chromosome and half carry a Y chromosome. This means it is the sperm, not the egg, that decides the sex of a baby.

At fertilisation an egg (always X) joins with a sperm. If the sperm carries an X chromosome the zygote is XX and develops into a girl. If the sperm carries a Y chromosome the zygote is XY and develops into a boy. Since X and Y sperm are made in equal numbers, the chance of any one fertilisation producing a boy is 1 in 2, the same as producing a girl.

You can show this with a genetic cross. Write the parents' sex chromosomes (XX × XY), then the possible gametes from each parent (X and X from the mother; X and Y from the father), then combine them in a Punnett square. The four boxes give XX, XX, XY and XY. So the expected ratio of female to male offspring is 2 : 2, which simplifies to 1 : 1. As a probability this is 0.5 or 50% for each sex, which can also be written as a fraction (1/2).

Each pregnancy is an independent event, so the sexes of previous children have no effect on the next one. A couple with three daughters still has a 50% chance that their next child will be a boy. Expected ratios are only predictions: in a small family the actual numbers can be very different from 1 : 1, but in a large population, such as thousands of births, the numbers of males and females come out very close to equal. You should be able to use direct proportion and simple ratios, for example predicting that about 300 of 600 babies will be girls.
keyFacts: Human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total).
22 pairs control characteristics only; 1 pair carries the genes that determine sex.
Females have two of the same sex chromosome: XX.
Males have two different sex chromosomes: XY.
All egg cells carry an X chromosome.
Half of sperm cells carry an X chromosome and half carry a Y chromosome.
The sperm determines the sex of the baby.
The expected ratio of female to male offspring is 1 : 1 (a 50% chance of each).
Each fertilisation is independent: earlier children do not change the probability for the next.

keyTerms.definition: The pair of chromosomes that carries the genes determining sex: XX in human females and XY in human males.
The larger sex chromosome. Females have two; males have one.
The smaller sex chromosome, found only in males (XY).
A sex cell (egg or sperm) containing one chromosome from each pair, so 23 chromosomes in humans, including one sex chromosome.
A diagram showing how the alleles or chromosomes of two parents can combine in their offspring, often drawn as a Punnett square.
A grid used to show all the possible combinations of gametes from two parents and so predict the ratio of offspring types.
The chance of an outcome happening, written as a fraction, decimal, percentage or ratio. For sex in humans it is 1/2, 0.5 or 50%.

workedExamples.title: Drawing a genetic cross for sex inheritance
workedExamples.question: Use a Punnett square to show the probability that a couple's child will be a girl.
steps: Write the parents' sex chromosomes: mother XX, father XY.
Write the gametes: the mother's eggs are X and X; the father's sperm are X and Y.
Fill in the Punnett square: X + X = XX, X + Y = XY, X + X = XX, X + Y = XY.
Count the outcomes: 2 out of 4 are XX (female).
workedExamples.answer: The probability of a girl is 1/2 (0.5 or 50%); the ratio of girls to boys is 1 : 1.

workedExamples.title: Using direct proportion
workedExamples.question: A hospital records 840 births in a year. Predict how many of the babies will be boys.
steps: The expected proportion of boys is 1/2.
workedExamples.answer: About 420 boys (the real number will be close to this but not necessarily exact).

workedExamples.title: Independent events
workedExamples.question: A couple already have three sons. What is the probability that their fourth child will be a girl?
steps: Each fertilisation is independent: the earlier children do not affect which sperm fertilises the next egg.
Half of the father's sperm carry X and half carry Y.
So the chance of the next child being XX is still 1/2.
workedExamples.answer: 1/2 (50%), the same as for any child.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the mother's egg decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl.
misconceptions.right: In fact every egg carries an X chromosome. The sperm carries either X or Y, so the sperm determines the sex.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that a couple who already have several girls are more likely to have a boy next.
misconceptions.right: In fact each fertilisation is independent. The probability of a boy is 50% for every child, whatever came before.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all 23 pairs of chromosomes are sex chromosomes, or that the sex chromosomes only control sex.
misconceptions.right: In fact only one of the 23 pairs is the sex chromosome pair; the other 22 pairs carry genes controlling other characteristics.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a 1 : 1 ratio means a family of four children must have exactly two girls and two boys.
misconceptions.right: In fact a ratio gives the expected proportion. Small samples often differ from it; only large numbers of births come out close to 1 : 1.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that a sperm cell carries 'XY'.
misconceptions.right: In fact a gamete carries only one sex chromosome, so each sperm carries either X or Y, never both.

realWorld: Hospitals and national statistics record roughly equal numbers of male and female births each year, matching the predicted 1 : 1 ratio across large populations.
Doctors and genetic counsellors use genetic crosses to explain to families the chance of a child being a boy or a girl, which matters for conditions carried on the X chromosome.
Karyotypes (photographs of a person's chromosomes arranged in pairs) are used in medicine to check the number of chromosomes, including the sex chromosomes.
examTips: When drawing a genetic cross, always show the parents' chromosomes, the gametes (circled) and the offspring. Marks are often given for each stage.
Write gametes as single letters (X or Y). A sperm or egg never carries XX or XY.
Read what form the question wants the probability in: ratio (1 : 1), fraction (1/2), decimal (0.5) or percentage (50%).
For 'how many' questions use direct proportion: multiply the total number by the probability, for example 500 × 0.5 = 250.
If asked which parent determines sex, explain why: eggs all carry X, while sperm carry X or Y.
summary: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; one pair is the sex chromosomes.
Females are XX and males are XY.
Eggs all carry X; sperm carry X or Y in equal numbers.
The sperm determines the sex of the offspring.
A Punnett square of XX × XY gives a 1 : 1 ratio of female to male.
The probability of either sex is 0.5 for every child, independently.

questions.question: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
markScheme: 1 mark: XY
questions.explanation: Males have two different sex chromosomes, X and Y. XX is female. YY does not occur because every person gets an X from their mother. A body cell always has a pair, so 'X only' is wrong.

questions.question: How many pairs of chromosomes are found in an ordinary human body cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 23
questions.explanation: Human body cells contain 23 pairs (46 chromosomes in total). 46 is the number of chromosomes, not pairs. 22 is the number of pairs that control characteristics only.

questions.question: Which sex chromosome is carried by every human egg cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: X
questions.explanation: Females are XX, so whichever chromosome of the pair goes into the egg, it is an X. Only sperm can carry Y. A gamete carries one sex chromosome, never both.

questions.question: Which of these determines whether a baby is male or female?
options: The number of chromosomes in the egg
markScheme: 1 mark: the sperm cell
questions.explanation: Eggs always carry X, but sperm carry either X or Y. So the sperm that fertilises the egg decides whether the zygote is XX (female) or XY (male). Temperature does not determine sex in humans.

questions.question: What proportion of a man's sperm cells carry a Y chromosome?
markScheme: 1 mark: half of them
questions.explanation: A man is XY. During meiosis the X and Y separate, so half of the sperm get the X and half get the Y.

questions.question: How many of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in a human body cell carry genes that control characteristics only, and not sex?
markScheme: 1 mark: 22
questions.explanation: 22 pairs control characteristics only. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes, which carry the genes that determine sex.

questions.question: A couple have four daughters. What is the probability that their next child will be a son?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.5
questions.explanation: Each fertilisation is independent. Half of the father's sperm carry Y, so the chance of a son is 0.5 every time. Previous children do not make a son 'due'.

questions.question: Which row correctly shows the sex chromosomes in a human sperm cell and a human egg cell?
options: Sperm: X or Y; egg: X or Y
Sperm: X or Y; egg: X
markScheme: 1 mark: sperm X or Y; egg X
questions.explanation: Gametes carry one sex chromosome. Eggs come from an XX parent so all carry X. Sperm come from an XY parent so each carries X or Y. Not all sperm carry Y.

questions.question: A Punnett square is drawn for the cross XX × XY. How many of the four boxes contain XY?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: The gametes are X, X (mother) and X, Y (father). Combining gives XX, XY, XX, XY: two of the four boxes are XY.

questions.question: A family has two children. What is the probability that both children are girls?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.25
questions.explanation: Each birth is independent with probability 0.5 of a girl. For both to be girls: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. The outcomes GG, GB, BG and BB are equally likely, and only one of the four is two girls.

questions.question: A student says: 'In a village where 10 babies were born last year, 7 were boys, so the 1 : 1 ratio must be wrong.' Which is the best response?
options: The student is right: the sperm must favour Y
The sample is too small; chance variation is large in small samples, and large samples come out close to 1 : 1
The ratio only applies to first-born children
The mothers must have produced more Y eggs
markScheme: 1 mark: sample too small, chance variation; large samples approach 1 : 1
questions.explanation: A ratio is an expected proportion. With only 10 births, results like 7 : 3 happen quite often by chance. Across thousands of births the ratio is very close to 1 : 1. Eggs never carry Y.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are in a human sperm cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 23
questions.explanation: Gametes contain one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs, so 46 ÷ 2 = 23. One of these is a sex chromosome (X or Y).

questions.question: What is the percentage chance that a couple's next baby will be a girl?
questions.explanation: The Punnett square XX × XY gives 2 XX out of 4, which is 2/4 = 1/2 = 50%.

questions.question: A maternity unit expects 1260 births next year. Using the expected ratio of male to female births, calculate the number of girls expected.
markScheme: 1 mark: proportion of girls = 1/2 (or 0.5)
questions.explanation: The ratio of girls to boys is 1 : 1, so half are expected to be girls: 1260 ÷ 2 = 630.

questions.question: How many of the chromosomes in a human body cell are not sex chromosomes? Give the number of chromosomes, not pairs.
markScheme: 1 mark: 44
questions.explanation: There are 22 pairs that are not sex chromosomes: 22 × 2 = 44. Adding the 2 sex chromosomes gives the total of 46.

questions.question: A couple plan to have three children. Calculate the probability that all three will be boys. Give your answer as a decimal.
markScheme: 1 mark: probability of a boy each time = 0.5
questions.explanation: Each child is an independent event with probability 0.5 of being a boy. Multiply for three events: 0.5³ = 0.125 (1/8, or 12.5%).

questions.question: In a survey of 2400 births, 1176 were girls. Calculate the percentage of births that were boys.
questions.explanation: Number of boys = 2400 − 1176 = 1224. Percentage = 1224 ÷ 2400 × 100 = 51%. This is close to the expected 50%, as you would predict for a large sample.

questions.question: State the sex chromosomes of a human female.
markScheme: 1 mark: XX
questions.explanation: Females have two of the same sex chromosome, XX.

questions.question: Name the type of diagram that is used to show all the possible combinations of gametes from two parents.
markScheme: 1 mark: Punnett square (allow genetic diagram or genetic cross)
questions.explanation: A Punnett square is a grid with one parent's gametes across the top and the other parent's down the side; the boxes show the possible offspring.

questions.question: What do the 22 pairs of chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes carry genes for?
markScheme: 1 mark: characteristics (other than sex) only
questions.explanation: The 22 non-sex pairs carry genes that control characteristics only. Only the 23rd pair carries the genes that determine sex.

questions.question: Explain why it is the father's sperm, and not the mother's egg, that determines the sex of a baby.
acceptedAnswers: mother is XX father is XY
markScheme: 1 mark: (mother is XX so) all eggs carry an X chromosome
1 mark: (father is XY so) sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome (half each)
questions.explanation: The egg always contributes an X, so it cannot change the outcome. Whether the zygote is XX or XY depends on whether the sperm carries X or Y.

questions.question: Complete a genetic cross for a man (XY) and a woman (XX). Give the gametes from each parent and the possible offspring.
markScheme: 1 mark: woman's gametes X and X
1 mark: man's gametes X and Y
1 mark: offspring XX, XX, XY, XY (or XX and XY in equal numbers)
questions.explanation: Separate each parent's pair into single gametes, then combine every egg with every sperm. Half of the offspring are XX (girls) and half are XY (boys).

questions.question: A couple have had three boys. They say their next child is 'bound to be a girl'. Explain why they are wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: each fertilisation / pregnancy is independent (previous children have no effect)
1 mark: the chance of a girl is still 50% (0.5, 1 in 2)
questions.explanation: Which sperm fertilises the egg is down to chance each time. Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y, so the probability is always 1/2.

questions.question: Describe how the sex chromosomes of a male differ from those of a female.
markScheme: 1 mark: females have two X chromosomes (XX), which are the same
1 mark: males have one X and one Y (XY), which are different
questions.explanation: In females both sex chromosomes are X. In males they are different: one X and one (smaller) Y.

questions.question: A family has four children: three girls and one boy. A student says this proves that girls are more likely to be born than boys. Evaluate this claim.
markScheme: 1 mark: the expected ratio from XX × XY is 1 : 1 (probability 0.5 each)
1 mark: four children is far too small a sample; chance variation is large
1 mark: conclusion: the claim is not supported; data from a large number of births is needed (which shows close to 1 : 1)
questions.explanation: Predicted ratios are probabilities. In small families, outcomes such as 3 : 1 occur by chance quite often. Only large samples give results close to the expected 1 : 1.

questions.question: Explain why no human can have the sex chromosomes YY.
acceptedAnswers: mother can only pass on X
at least one X from mother
markScheme: 1 mark: each person inherits one sex chromosome from each parent
1 mark: the mother (XX) can only pass on an X, so everyone has at least one X
questions.explanation: One sex chromosome comes from the egg and one from the sperm. All eggs carry X, so the zygote always has at least one X: it can only be XX or XY.

questions.question: Use a genetic cross to explain why, in a large population, roughly equal numbers of boys and girls are born.
markScheme: Indicative content: mother is XX and father is XY; gametes are made by meiosis so each has one sex chromosome; all eggs carry X; half of sperm carry X and half carry Y; Punnett square shows XX, XX, XY, XY; XX is female and XY is male; ratio 1 : 1 or probability 0.5; each fertilisation is random/independent; in large numbers the actual ratio is close to the expected ratio.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct genetic cross with gametes and offspring, linked to the 1 : 1 ratio and the idea that large numbers make the actual result close to the prediction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states the parents' or offspring sex chromosomes or the 50% chance, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: The key steps are parents (XX × XY), gametes (X, X and X, Y), offspring (2 XX : 2 XY) and the 1 : 1 conclusion. Mentioning that a large sample is needed for the real result to match the prediction lifts the answer.

questions.question: Describe how sex is inherited in humans. Your answer should include the chromosomes in body cells and gametes, how fertilisation determines sex, and the probability of each sex.
markScheme: Indicative content: human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46); 22 pairs control characteristics only; one pair is the sex chromosomes; females are XX and males are XY; gametes are made by meiosis and contain 23 chromosomes, one from each pair; eggs all contain X; sperm contain X or Y in equal numbers; at fertilisation an X sperm gives XX (girl) and a Y sperm gives XY (boy); sperm therefore determines sex; Punnett square gives 2 XX : 2 XY; ratio 1 : 1, probability 0.5 or 50%; each fertilisation is independent; large populations show close to 1 : 1.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically sequenced description covering chromosome numbers in body cells and gametes, the gametes from each parent, fertilisation outcomes and a correct probability or ratio.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes XX/XY and some gamete or fertilisation detail, with a ratio or probability, but with gaps in the sequence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'females are XX and males are XY' with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers move logically from body cells (23 pairs, XX or XY) to gametes (eggs X; sperm X or Y), to fertilisation (XX or XY), to the probability (0.5 each, 1 : 1), and point out that the sperm decides.
